question: What is the difference between Container, SizedBox, Padding, and ColoredBox?
answer:
SizedBox, Padding and ColoredBox each do exactly one job; Container is a convenience wrapper that composes several of them at once.

• SizedBox — constraints only (width/height). The lightest spacer.
• Padding — adds padding, nothing else. Cheaper than a Container for the same effect.
• ColoredBox — sets a background colour only.
• DecoratedBox — border, shadow or gradient, without touching size.
• Container — sizing, padding, margin, decoration and transform in one widget. It builds those intermediate widgets internally, so reach for it only when you actually need several at once.

There is also a const-ness cost: Container has no const constructor, so it can never be a const widget, while `const SizedBox(...)`, `const Padding(...)` and `const ColoredBox(...)` all can — and const widgets are skipped entirely during a rebuild.

question: Explain Row, Column, and Stack with their key properties.
answer:
Row lays its children out horizontally, Column vertically, and Stack overlaps them along the z-axis.

Row/Column key properties:
• mainAxisAlignment: start, end, center, spaceBetween, spaceAround, spaceEvenly
• crossAxisAlignment: start, end, center, stretch, baseline
• mainAxisSize: max (fill the available space) or min (wrap the children)

Stack key properties:
• alignment — where non-positioned children sit
• fit — StackFit.loose (children pick their own size) or StackFit.expand
• Positioned — absolute placement inside the Stack

Row and Column hand their children unbounded space along the main axis, which is why an unconstrained child — a nested ListView, a long Text — produces the classic yellow-and-black overflow stripes. Wrap it in Expanded or Flexible.

question: What is the difference between ListView, GridView, and CustomScrollView?
answer:
ListView scrolls along a single axis, GridView lays out a scrollable 2D grid, and CustomScrollView stitches several sliver areas into one coordinated scroll.

ListView:
• ListView() — builds every child immediately; only for short, fixed lists
• ListView.builder() — lazy, and the right default for long or infinite lists
• ListView.separated() — builder plus a separator between items

GridView:
• GridView.count() — a fixed number of columns
• GridView.builder() — lazy, efficient
• GridView.extent() — columns derived from a maximum cross-axis extent

CustomScrollView takes slivers rather than widgets — SliverAppBar, SliverList, SliverGrid, SliverToBoxAdapter — and is the only way to make a collapsing header and a list scroll as one. It is the most flexible option and also the most verbose, so use it when a plain ListView genuinely cannot express the layout.

question: How do you handle forms and validation in Flutter?
answer:
A Form widget plus a GlobalKey<FormState> coordinates validation and saving across every field inside it.

• Form — wraps the fields and exposes validate, save and reset through its FormState
• TextFormField — a TextField wired into the Form, with a validator callback
• FormField<T> — the base class for building a custom form field

Validation flow:
1. The user taps submit
2. _formKey.currentState!.validate() runs every field validator and paints the error text
3. If that returned true, _formKey.currentState!.save() runs the onSaved callbacks
4. Collect the data and proceed

A validator returns null when the value is valid, or the error string to display. Set autovalidateMode: AutovalidateMode.onUserInteraction so a field only complains after the user has touched it, rather than showing errors on a form the user has not filled in yet.

question: How does CustomPainter work and when would you use it?
answer:
CustomPainter gives you direct access to a Canvas to draw anything — shapes, paths, gradients, charts — that built-in widgets cannot achieve.

Steps:
1. Extend CustomPainter and implement paint() and shouldRepaint()
2. Use the CustomPaint widget, passing your painter
3. Draw with the Canvas API: drawLine, drawCircle, drawPath, drawRect, drawArc, drawImage, and drawParagraph for text (laid out first with TextPainter)

shouldRepaint() controls when to repaint:
• Return false when the visual output has not changed — this is a real optimization, not a formality
• Return true only when a property that affects the drawing has changed

Canvas coordinates start at (0,0) in the top-left, and the size argument gives you the widget's width and height. Wrap the CustomPaint in a RepaintBoundary when the painter animates, so a repaint does not drag the rest of the screen with it.

question: What is the difference between Expanded and Flexible widgets?
answer:
Expanded is the tight form of Flexible — it forces its child to fill exactly the space it was allotted.

Flexible:
• fit: FlexFit.loose (the default) — the child may end up smaller than its share
• fit: FlexFit.tight — identical to Expanded
• flex decides the share of the free space

Expanded:
• Shorthand for Flexible(fit: FlexFit.tight)
• The child's own size along the main axis is ignored
• The form you will see in most real code

flex, on both:
• Defaults to 1
• Shares are proportional to the sum of the flex values among siblings
• flex: 2 gets twice the space of flex: 1

Both only work as a direct child of Row, Column or Flex, and throw anywhere else. Spacer is nothing more than an Expanded wrapped around an empty SizedBox.

question: What are the Material 3 button widgets and when do you pick each?
answer:
Material 3 ships five button styles, each with a specific role on the page. Picking the right one is the difference between a clear UI and visual noise.

FilledButton (highest emphasis):
• Solid background, used for the PRIMARY action on a screen
• Examples: "Sign up", "Continue", "Pay now"

FilledButton.tonal (high-emphasis but secondary):
• Tinted background, used for important actions that aren't the primary
• Good when the screen has two important options and you don't want them visually competing

ElevatedButton (legacy primary):
• Drop shadow, originally THE primary button style in Material 2
• In Material 3, prefer FilledButton — ElevatedButton is for cases where elevation specifically matches the material

OutlinedButton (medium emphasis):
• Outlined, transparent fill — the secondary button on a page
• Cancel/Back/Skip alongside a FilledButton

TextButton (lowest emphasis):
• Text only, no border or background
• "Forgot password?", "Learn more", in-line actions in cards

IconButton:
• Square button containing only an icon
• Use `IconButton.filled`, `.filledTonal`, `.outlined` for the matching emphasis levels

Rules of thumb:
• At most ONE FilledButton per screen — that's the primary action
• Use the same button type for consistent CTAs across screens
• Don't sprinkle ElevatedButton everywhere — Material 3 favors flatter UI

question: How do you display images in Flutter — assets, network, memory, file?
answer:
Flutter's `Image` widget renders any image source via constructors that match the input.

Image.asset — bundled with the app:
• Add to pubspec.yaml under `flutter: assets:`
• Supports @1x, @2x, @3x variants for resolution-aware loading
• No network needed; instant

Image.network — fetched at runtime:
• Includes basic in-memory cache only; for offline + disk cache use `cached_network_image`
• `errorBuilder` for fallback when the URL fails

Image.memory — render bytes you already have:
• Useful for downloaded blobs, captured screenshots, base64-decoded images

Image.file — local files (path_provider, picked images):
• Mobile/desktop only; not on web

Key props for any source:
• `fit: BoxFit.cover/contain/fill/...` — how the image fits its box
• `width / height` — display size; combine with `cacheWidth / cacheHeight` to avoid decoding the full source for a thumbnail
• `loadingBuilder` for progressive loading spinners
• `semanticLabel` for accessibility

For SVGs use `flutter_svg` (Image doesn't render SVG); for animated formats (Lottie, Rive) use the dedicated packages.

question: How does LayoutBuilder work and when should you use it?
answer:
LayoutBuilder provides parent constraints to build child widgets responsively.

Key features:
• Receives BoxConstraints from parent
• Builds child based on available space
• Useful for responsive layouts
• Rebuilds when constraints change

Constraints:
• maxWidth, maxHeight — maximum available
• minWidth, minHeight — minimum required
• Use to build adaptive UI

Similar widgets:
• MediaQuery — entire screen size
• LayoutBuilder — parent-specific constraints
• OrientationBuilder — device orientation

question: How do you make an arbitrary widget tappable, and when is InkWell the better choice over GestureDetector?
answer:
GestureDetector recognises the gesture but draws nothing, while InkWell adds the Material ripple plus hover and focus feedback.

GestureDetector:
• Handles taps, double taps, long presses, drags, scales and pans
• Purely functional, so a tap on it looks like nothing happened
• Right choice for custom gestures and for non-Material surfaces

InkWell and InkResponse:
• Paint a splash, a highlight and a focus ring, and carry button semantics for screen readers
• The splash is painted onto the nearest Material ancestor, so an InkWell placed over a coloured Container shows no ripple — the Container paints on top of it. Use `Ink(color: ...)` instead of the Container's colour, or wrap the whole thing in a Material.
• `borderRadius` should match the surrounding shape, otherwise the splash spills over the rounded corners

Before either one, check whether a real widget already does the job: FilledButton, TextButton, IconButton, ListTile, Card and Chip all take an onTap or onPressed and come with the correct feedback and semantics for free.

The trap people hit is hit testing. A GestureDetector only receives taps where its child actually paints, so an empty area or a Container with no colour swallows nothing and the tap goes through. `behavior: HitTestBehavior.opaque` makes the whole box tappable; `translucent` lets a widget behind it also receive the event.

One last thing: a bare GestureDetector is invisible to accessibility tools. Wrap it in `Semantics(button: true, label: ...)` when it acts as a button.

question: What is the difference between implicit and explicit animations in Flutter, and which should you reach for first?
answer:
An implicit animation interpolates a property for you whenever its value changes, while an explicit one hands you an AnimationController that you drive yourself.

Implicit — the default choice:
• AnimatedContainer, AnimatedOpacity, AnimatedPadding, AnimatedAlign, AnimatedPositioned, AnimatedDefaultTextStyle
• You change the value inside setState and pass a `duration` and a `curve`; the widget animates from the old value to the new one
• AnimatedSwitcher animates between two different children, and needs a Key on the child so it can tell that the child really changed
• TweenAnimationBuilder covers a one-off custom property without a controller
• No controller, no ticker, nothing to dispose

Explicit — when you need control:
• AnimationController with `vsync: this` from SingleTickerProviderStateMixin, plus a Tween and usually a CurvedAnimation
• Necessary for repeating or reversing, for starting and stopping on demand, for `fling` with a velocity, for staggering several animations off one controller, and for gesture-driven motion
• Drive the UI with FadeTransition, SlideTransition, ScaleTransition or AnimatedBuilder rather than reading `controller.value` in build — the transition widgets skip the rebuild and only repaint
• Always dispose the controller

Rule of thumb: if you can express the change as "this property has a new value, animate to it", use the implicit widget. Reach for a controller only when the animation has a life of its own. Keep durations short, around a couple of hundred milliseconds, and respect `MediaQuery.disableAnimationsOf` for users who ask for reduced motion.

question: Putting a ListView inside a Column throws a layout error. What causes it and what are the fixes?
answer:
A Column gives its children unbounded height on the main axis, and a ListView tries to fill whatever height it is given, so together they produce an infinite constraint.

The message is usually "Vertical viewport was given unbounded height" or a RenderBox that was not laid out. Same story for a horizontal ListView inside a Row.

The fixes, best first:
• Expanded around the ListView when it should take the space that is left. This keeps lazy building and gives the list its own scrollbar.
• A SizedBox with a fixed height when the list is a band of a known size, which is also how you place a horizontal ListView inside a Column.
• `shrinkWrap: true` together with `physics: NeverScrollableScrollPhysics()` when the list is short and the OUTER widget does the scrolling. shrinkWrap measures every child up front, so it silently kills the laziness that ListView.builder exists for — acceptable for ten rows, never for a feed.
• A CustomScrollView with SliverToBoxAdapter for the header and SliverList for the items. This is the real answer to "a header plus a long list": one scroll gesture, one viewport, and the list stays lazy.

Two related traps:
• Nesting two scrollables on the same axis makes them fight for the drag; the inner one wins. NestedScrollView exists for the collapsing-app-bar case, not as a general fix.
• Wrapping the Column in a SingleChildScrollView removes the overflow stripes but does not help the inner ListView — the height is still unbounded.
